summary: Make any server able to handle the next request by storing user state outside the server.
goals: What “state” means and why it ties a user to one server
Sticky sessions and what happens when a server fails
How a shared session store lets any server handle a user
How a signed token can carry identity
Why uploaded files belong in object storage

body: Alice signs in and adds two items to her cart. Her request reaches Server A, which keeps a session in memory: information about her login and cart. Her browser stores a cookie with the session ID, which later requests use to find that session.
steps.callout: State is information a server remembers between requests, such as a login, a cart, or an unfinished upload.
When one server keeps a user’s state only in its own memory, the other servers cannot use that state.
Sticky sessions keep a user on one server. If many users stick to the same server, it can be overloaded while others sit idle.
With sticky sessions, each server becomes a single point of failure for the users assigned to it.

body: Keep sessions in a shared, fast session store, often Redis. Every server can read Alice’s session from this store, so any server can handle her request. The application servers are now stateless: they do not keep user information between requests. The load balancer can send requests to any server, and Alice stays signed in.
steps.callout: The shared store adds about one millisecond to a request. In return, you can add, remove, or lose application servers more easily.
Stateless servers can be replaced without losing a user’s session. This also makes it easier to add or remove servers as traffic changes.

body: Another option is to put some state in each request as a signed token. For example, a JSON Web Token (JWT) can identify Alice. Any server can check the token’s signature without looking up a session. This avoids a shared-store lookup, but a token is hard to cancel before it expires and travels with every request, so keep it small.
steps.callout: A common approach is to use tokens for identity and a shared store for larger or quickly changing data, such as carts or revoked logins.
Anything saved only on one server’s disk—uploads, generated PDFs, or temporary files—is unavailable to other servers. It is also lost when that server is replaced.

body: Store files in shared object storage, such as Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage. It is designed to store durable files that every server can access. Server A saves the avatar there, and B and C can read the same file. A browser can also fetch images through a CDN.
steps.callout: Rule of thumb: servers should not keep information that must survive a request. Put sessions in a shared store or token, files in object storage, and application data in a database.

body:
• State kept only in a server’s memory ties the user to that server.
  • Sticky sessions hide the problem until that server fails.
  • Move state to a shared store or carry some of it in a signed token.
  • Store files in object storage, not on one server’s local disk.
  • Stateless servers can be added, removed, or replaced more easily.
steps.callout: Next: Caching — the database used by these stateless servers can become a bottleneck.
